title: One Obstruction, Three Faces — Merle Lean stack, with Lean 4 formalisations of Halbeisen–Hungerbühler 1997, Lagarias 1990 and Steiner 1978
description:
Lean 4 verification stack of Eric Merle (the “kernel key”) for the joint note One obstruction, three faces with Benjamin Macindoe, together with Lean 4 formalisations of two classical papers: L. Halbeisen and N. Hungerbühler, “Optimal bounds for the length of rational Collatz cycles”, Acta Arithmetica 78 (1997), 227–239, and J. C. Lagarias, “The set of rational cycles for the 3x+1 problem”, Acta Arithmetica 56 (1990), 33–53; and of a classical theorem, R. P. Steiner, “A theorem on the Syracuse problem”, Congressus Numerantium 20 (1978), 553–559, reconstructed from published accounts.

hh1997/ (Lean 4.34.0, Mathlib v4.34.0): every result that the paper proves is kernel-checked (70 proved statements, each frozen before its proof was written), with no sorry in the proofs, no native_decide, and only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. One statement of the paper, Remark 1 for l > 10³, is stated and not proved, since the paper gives no proof; Remark 2 and two figures the paper quotes from other authors are not formalised. The formalisation proves nothing new about Collatz cycles. See hh1997/README.md, which also lists the points found in the paper.

lagarias1990/ (Lean 4.34.0, Mathlib v4.34.0): 60 frozen statements, all proved (61 theorems, since Corollary 2.1a is proved twice), each statement written before its proof (git records this order for the last six), with no sorry in the proofs, no native_decide, and only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Theorem 3.1 with the printed constant and Theorem 3.2 are proved under named hypotheses (the prime number theorem; the bound (3.3), a consequence of the Baker–Fel’dman bound), which are hypotheses of the theorems, not axioms; Theorem 3.1 is also proved without any hypothesis, with the constant 6/5 instead of 5/4. Out of scope: Theorems 3.3 and 4.3, the bounds (4.12)–(4.14), Remarks (2)–(4) of p. 52 with (4.19), and the flat segment of Fig. 4.1. The minimality of the 48 unchanged rows of Table 3.1 is checked numerically, not in Lean. For the results in scope, where we found a slip in a printed statement or proof, the repaired version is proved; the slips found are listed next to what is printed in lagarias1990/README.md, and the list is not exhaustive. The formalisation proves nothing new about Collatz cycles.

steiner1978/ (Lean 4.34.0, Mathlib v4.34.0): the original paper could not be accessed and was not read; the statements are reconstructed from R. Steiner, Fibonacci Quarterly 19 (1981), 285–288, J. C. Lagarias’s annotated bibliography of the 3x+1 problem (entries 48, 158, 159) and J. Simons and B. de Weger, Acta Arithmetica 117 (2005), read in their version 1.44 (2010), §1.4 and Lemma 12. 12 frozen statements, all proved, each statement written before its proof, with no sorry in the proofs, no native_decide, and only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Steiner’s theorem (the only circuit on the positive integers that is a cycle of the 3x+1 map is {1, 2}) is proved under a named hypothesis, the case u₀ = 0 of G. Rhin’s inequality (7) (Progress in Mathematics 71, 1987), which is a hypothesis of the theorems, not an axiom. Without any hypothesis it is proved for at most 20000 odd terms, by a finite check certified by the kernel; this is far weaker than the published bounds that rest on computer verifications of the conjecture. The formalisation proves nothing new about Collatz cycles.

The rest of the repository is the Merle side of the joint note; the status of each of its entries is the claims ledger of the shared repository macindoe/one-obstruction-three-faces, not this archive. Its six Lean files were first checked on Lean 4.27.0 and re-checked on Lean 4.34.0 (recheck-v4.34/RECHECK.md). Nothing in this repository excludes a Collatz cycle beyond the published bounds (Bařina's verification to 2^71; Hercher 2023).
